sections.content: Why Semantic Elements?

Before HTML5, developers used <div id='header'>, <div id='nav'> etc. for everything. Now dedicated semantic elements exist. They tell the browser, search engines, and screen readers exactly what each section does — without relying on CSS class names.
💡 Semantic HTML is the single biggest thing you can do for accessibility and SEO with zero extra effort.
header, nav, footer

<header> represents the introductory content of a page or section — typically a logo, site title, and navigation. <nav> wraps sets of navigation links. <footer> contains information like copyright, contact links, or secondary navigation at the bottom of a page or section.

exercises.question: Build a page header with a site title 'TechBlog' inside an h1, and a nav with links to 'Home', 'Articles', and 'Contact'.
hints: The site title should be in <h1>
exercises.explanation: header and nav are semantic landmarks. Assistive technologies announce these to users so they can jump directly to navigation.

exercises.question: Which element is best for wrapping a site's primary navigation links?
hints: Think semantic — the element name should describe its purpose
exercises.explanation: <nav> is the dedicated semantic element for navigation links. div with a class is non-semantic and requires extra ARIA to be accessible.

sections.content: main — The Unique Content Area

<main> wraps the primary, unique content of the page. There should only be one <main> per page, and it should not include repeated content like navigation or footers. Screen reader users can skip directly to <main> to bypass navigation.
section vs article

Both are block-level semantic containers but they serve different purposes. Use <article> for self-contained content that makes sense on its own — blog posts, news articles, comments, product cards. Use <section> to group thematically related content within a page that doesn't stand alone.

sections.content: aside — Related but Not Essential

<aside> contains content tangentially related to the main content. Think sidebars with related articles, author bios, pull quotes, or advertisements. The key test: if removed, does the main content still make complete sense? If yes — it belongs in <aside>.

figure & figcaption
<figure> wraps self-contained content like images, diagrams, code samples, or charts that are referenced from the main content but could be moved. <figcaption> provides a caption for the figure.

sections.content: The time Element

The <time> element represents a specific point in time or a date. The datetime attribute provides a machine-readable format (ISO 8601), while the content can be human-readable. This helps search engines display accurate publish dates and enables features like 'Posted 3 days ago'.

mark, details, summary

<mark> highlights text for reference — like search results highlighted in a document. <details> creates a native disclosure widget that can expand/collapse without JavaScript. <summary> is its visible clickable label.

exercises.question: Which element highlights text as being relevant to the current context (e.g. search results)?
hints: It literally looks like a highlighter marker
exercises.explanation: <mark> semantically highlights text for relevance. <em> adds emphasis, <strong> adds importance. Neither is for highlighting search terms.

sections.content: What is ARIA?

ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) is a set of HTML attributes that make web content more accessible to people using assistive technologies like screen readers. The first rule of ARIA: don't use ARIA if native HTML does the job. Use semantic elements first.
Essential ARIA Attributes

aria-label provides an accessible name when no visible label exists. aria-hidden='true' hides decorative elements from screen readers. aria-expanded indicates whether a component is open/closed. role overrides or adds semantic meaning when a native element is not available.
• Home
⚠️ Testing tip: Use your keyboard alone (Tab, Enter, Space, Arrow keys) to navigate your site. If you get stuck, that's an accessibility bug.
